item.title: Korean Jjimjilbang Guide: How a Visit Works, Step by Step
item.description: Your first Korean jjimjilbang, step by step: shoe lockers, the uniform, the gender-separated baths, sauna rooms, sikhye and eggs, sleeping over, and etiquette.
item.content:encoded:
A Korean jjimjilbang is a bathhouse with gender-separated baths and shared heated sauna rooms. You store your shoes, take a locker key, shower and bathe naked in the baths, then put on the loose uniform for the common sauna rooms, snack bar and sleeping area. Many stay open 24 hours.

A jjimjilbang (찜질방) is a Korean bathhouse with heated rooms. You bathe, sweat in sauna rooms, eat, nap and sometimes stay the night, all in one building.

The Korea Herald describes it as a Korean-style sauna built on two old heating ideas: ondol, the heated floor, and gama, dome-shaped kiln rooms. The Korea Times notes that many are open 24 hours. It feels strange the first time. After that, it is simple.

How a visit works, step by step

  1. Take off your shoes. Do it at the entrance and put them in a small shoe locker. Keep the key.
  2. Pay at the counter. You hand over the shoe key, or show it, and get a locker key, a uniform and towels. The Korea Herald describes this order at one jjimjilbang.
  3. Go to your side. Men and women split here into separate locker rooms and baths.
  4. Undress fully. The baths are naked-only, Korea.net notes. Everyone around you is doing the same.
  5. Shower before you soak. Wash your whole body and hair at the shower stations. This is the rule that matters most.
  6. Bathe. Move between hot, warm and cold pools at your own pace. Drink water.
  7. Put on the uniform. It is usually a loose T-shirt and shorts. Now you can go to the shared floor.
  8. Use the sauna rooms. Men and women mix here, all in uniform.
  9. Eat, rest, sleep. Then shower again, return the uniform and towels, and pay any extras when you hand back your key.

The locker key does a lot

  • Wear it. VisitKorea notes that the key usually goes on your wrist or ankle.
  • It is your wallet. At many places it also pays for snacks and massage chairs, and you settle the total at the counter when you leave.

The sauna rooms

  • Different themes. Rooms are lined with clay, salt, stone, charcoal or jade, and some are cold rooms for cooling down.
  • Start cool. VisitKorea suggests first-timers start in rooms around 30 to 40°C.
  • Short stays in the hottest rooms. For rooms above 60°C, VisitKorea advises keeping it to about 20 minutes. Some kiln rooms ask you to cover your skin with a towel and wear clogs, the Korea Herald reports.
  • Leave if you feel dizzy. Rest, drink water and cool down.

Food: sikhye and eggs

  • Sikhye (식혜). A cold, sweet rice drink. The Korea Herald calls it a traditional drink made with rice and malt.
  • Roasted eggs. Eggs slow-cooked in the heat, called kiln-cooked eggs in the Korea Herald. VisitKorea calls sikhye with roasted eggs a popular, affordable pair.
  • Real meals too. Snack bars and restaurants sell noodles, soups and more. Some places let you bring food, others don’t, so check.

The towel hat

You will see people with a hand towel rolled into two side buns, called yangmeori (양머리), or “sheep head.” VisitKorea notes it is a familiar image from Korean media. It keeps your hair up and away from the heat. Roll a towel in thirds lengthwise, then roll each end in toward the middle, and set it on your head.

Sleeping over

The Korea Times describes napping or staying overnight on the heated floor among strangers as an ordinary Korean scene. Some places have mats or a quiet sleeping room. Keep valuables in your locker and ask at the counter whether staying overnight costs extra.

Tattoos

Rules vary by place. The Korea JoongAng Daily reports that some hotel and golf-course saunas refuse visible tattoos or ask guests to cover them with patches. If you have tattoos, check the counter sign or ask before you pay.

Entry prices and hours change, so check them at the counter or on the place’s Naver Map page.

Etiquette in short

  • Shower first, every time. Wash fully before any pool.
  • Keep towels out of the water. Tie long hair up.
  • No phones or photos in the bath and locker areas.
  • Keep your voice low in sauna rooms and sleeping areas.
  • Don't stare. Nudity is ordinary here.
  • Return what you borrow. Uniforms and towels go in the marked bins.

Adding a seshin body scrub

Many bathhouses offer a paid body scrub, called seshin (세신) or ttaemiri (때밀이). It is optional. CNN Travel's interviews with Seoul scrub attendants describe it like this:

  • Same-gender attendants scrub you in the bath area.
  • Soak first, about 30 minutes.
  • Bar soap before, not body wash.
  • About 40 minutes on a table, then a rinse.

Ask at the counter or the bath area. For doing it yourself with a scrub mitt, see our Italy towel guide.

What to bring

  • Not much. Towels and the uniform come with entry.
  • Your own toiletries if you are picky. Many places have basic soap, and some sell small packs.
  • A hair tie.
  • A card or cash for extras. Some places charge snacks to your locker key.
  • Moisturizer for after the heat. See our Korean body care picks.

item.title: Korean Head Spa: What Happens and How to Book in Seoul
item.description: What a Korean head spa visit usually includes, from the scalp camera check to the blow-dry, how long it takes, how to book in Seoul, and what to ask first.
item.content:encoded:
A Korean head spa is a scalp care session at a salon or spa. It usually starts with a close-up scalp check through a small camera, then cleansing, a scalp mask, a head and neck massage and a blow-dry. The Korea Herald says sessions usually run 60 to 90 minutes. Book ahead, often on Naver Map.

A Korean head spa is an appointment for your scalp. You lie back, someone looks at your scalp up close, cleans it slowly, massages your head and neck, and dries your hair.

Many visitors now plan one into a Seoul trip. The Korea Herald describes head and hair spas as a popular wellness stop for foreign visitors.

What a visit usually includes

Programs differ by shop, but most follow the same order. This is the sequence the Korea Herald describes, with the usual extras.

  • Consultation. A short form or chat about your scalp, hair history and what you want from the session.
  • Scalp check with a camera. The therapist moves a small handheld camera or microscope across your scalp and shows you the close-up on a screen. It is a look at oil, flakes and buildup, not a medical diagnosis.
  • Pre-treatment. A gel or tonic goes on to loosen buildup before washing.
  • Cleansing and scaling. A slow wash, often in a reclining chair, with tools or brushes that lift residue from the scalp.
  • Mask and massage. A scalp mask, then a hand massage of the head that often moves down to the neck and shoulders.
  • Rinse. Some shops finish with a long rinse of warm or herb-infused water poured over the head.
  • Blow-dry. A dry and light styling. Ask if you want it done a certain way.

How long it takes

  • About 60 to 90 minutes, according to the Korea Herald.
  • One hour is common for basic programs. A VisitKorea listing for one head spa, for example, gives 60 minutes for its scrub, serum and massage course.
  • More steps take longer. Shops sell programs by step count or by length. More steps do not always mean better care. Pick the program that fits the time you have.

How to book

  • Naver Map. Search 헤드스파 (head spa) near your hotel, open a shop’s page and tap the booking button. Since June 2026, the Korea Times reports, travelers can verify with a passport instead of a Korean phone number for Naver reservations and payments.
  • Booking apps and travel platforms. Many shops also sell slots through visitor booking sites in English. Read what the program includes before you pay.
  • Messages. Some shops answer through Instagram or KakaoTalk. Send the date, time and program you want.
  • Book ahead. Weekend slots can go first.

On the day

  • Arrive with unwashed hair if you like. Cleansing is part of the session.
  • Skip heavy styling products so the scalp check shows your usual scalp.
  • Bring a hair tie and remove earrings.
  • Say how you feel. If the water is too hot or the massage too strong, tell the therapist. “약하게 해 주세요” means “gently, please.”
  • No tip. Tipping is not customary in Korea, as we explain in our Seoul hair salon guide.

What a head spa is not

A head spa is a beauty and relaxation service. The shop is not a clinic, and the scalp camera does not diagnose anything. If you are worried about hair loss or a scalp condition, see a dermatologist. For products you can keep using at home, see our Korean scalp care guide, and for in-salon conditioning, our Korean hair treatment guide.

Prices change often and differ by shop and program, so check the total on the booking page before you go.

Questions to ask before you book

  • How long is this program? Step counts differ, and so does time.
  • What is the total? Ask whether the price changes with hair length or added treatments.
  • Is a blow-dry included? Some programs end with full styling, some with a quick dry.
  • Chair or bed? Some shops wash you lying back, some seated.
  • Is there English help? Many shops reply through Naver or social media messages.
  • Cancellation rules? Check the notice period before you pay a deposit.

Who should check first

  • Broken skin, sores or a sunburned scalp: wait until it heals.
  • A scalp condition such as psoriasis or seborrheic dermatitis: ask your dermatologist first.
  • Fresh bleach, perm or color: tell the therapist, since products and water heat may sting.
  • Allergies: ask to see the products, and mention fragrance or ingredient allergies.
  • Neck or back pain: ask for a lighter massage.

Words to know

  • 헤드스파 (he-deu-seu-pa): head spa.
  • 두피 케어 (du-pi ke-eo): scalp care.
  • 두피 진단 (du-pi jin-dan): scalp check.
  • 예약 (ye-yak): booking.
  • "약하게 해 주세요." (ya-ka-ge hae ju-se-yo) Gently, please.
  • "총 얼마예요?" (chong eol-ma-ye-yo?) What is the total?

item.title: Seoul Travel Tips for Your First Trip: What to Know
item.description: Seoul travel tips for a first trip: airport train or bus, the T-money card, which map and taxi apps work, cash or card, plugs, and why you don't tip.
item.content:encoded:
Ride the AREX airport train or an airport limousine bus into Seoul, buy a T-money card for subways and buses, and use Naver Map or KakaoMap for directions. Pay by card where you can, but carry some won for T-money top-ups. Korea uses 220V outlets with two round holes, and tipping is not expected, per Visit Seoul and VisitKorea.

A first trip to Seoul goes smoothly once a few small things are sorted: how you get in from the airport, how you pay for the subway, and which apps actually give you directions. None of it is hard. It just works a little differently from home.

Here is what to set up, in the order you will need it.

1. Airport to the city: train or bus

If you land at Incheon Airport, you have two easy options.

  • AREX Express train: runs non-stop between Incheon Airport and Seoul Station in about 43 minutes, Visit Seoul says (as of June 2026). Seats are reserved, and you buy a separate ticket before boarding.
  • AREX All-Stop train: takes about 59 minutes to Seoul Station and stops at Gimpo Airport, Hongik Univ. (Hongdae) and Gongdeok on the way, per Visit Seoul. It works like the subway, with unreserved seats.
  • Airport limousine bus: goes straight to areas such as Myeongdong, Hongdae, Jongno and Gangnam in about 60 to 80 minutes, Visit Seoul says. T-money is accepted, but ticket holders board first.
  • Luggage on the bus: Visit Seoul lists a limit of 2 bags per person, 28 inches or under (as of Nov. 17, 2026. Source: Visit Seoul).

Which one? Take the Express if your hotel is near Seoul Station. Take the All-Stop if you stay in Hongdae. Take the bus if you have big suitcases and your area has a direct route.

2. Get a T-money card

T-money is a tap card for subways, buses and taxis. You can buy it at the airport, subway vending machines and convenience stores, Visit Seoul says.

  • Seoul buses don’t take cash. Have a transport card ready (as of June 2026. Source: Visit Seoul).
  • Tap when you get on and when you get off. On buses, tapping out lets you transfer to another bus or the subway within 30 minutes at a discount, Visit Seoul says (as of June 2026).
  • Bring won to reload it. A physical T-money card can only be topped up with Korean won, the Korea Times reported. VisitKorea says the reload machines are inside subway stations.

3. Use a Korean map app

Google Maps has long been limited in Korea. The government approved Google’s request to export detailed map data in February 2026, with security conditions, but gave no launch date for full navigation, the Korea Times reported.

For now, use what locals use. VisitKorea recommends Naver Map and KakaoMap and says both offer navigation in English. Search the store or hotel name, then pick subway, bus or walking.

4. Taxis: hail one or use an app

Taxis take cash, credit cards or transportation cards, VisitKorea says.

  • k.ride is Kakao Mobility’s version of Kakao T for visitors, available in English, Chinese and Japanese. It accepts credit cards issued overseas, per VisitKorea.
  • Uber also works in Korea, and VisitKorea says the app translates messages to the driver.
  • Late at night, a surcharge usually applies from 22:00 to 04:00 (as of Nov. 17, 2026. Source: VisitKorea).

5. Cash or card

Pay by card where you can, and keep some won as a backup.

  • Foreign cards can fail at some terminals, and many Korean websites and apps reject them, the Korea Times reported in April 2025.
  • ATMs with a Global sign accept international cards, Visit Seoul says. Fees vary by ATM, so check the fee on screen before you confirm.
  • Banks usually give the best exchange rates, per Visit Seoul. Avoid uncertified exchange booths.

6. Plugs and voltage

Korea runs on 220 volts at 60 Hertz, and outlets have two round holes, VisitKorea says (as of Sept. 11, 2026). US plugs need an adapter.

  • Check your chargers. A label that reads “100-240V” means the charger handles 220V with just a plug adapter. If it says only 110-120V, it needs a voltage converter.
  • Forgot one? VisitKorea says hotels may lend or sell adapters, and the airport, convenience stores and duty-free shops sell them.

7. Tipping is not expected

Visit Seoul says tipping is not a Korean custom. Many major hotels and upscale restaurants add a 10 percent service charge instead. In taxis, you pay what the meter says.

Apps to download before you fly

  • Naver Map: routes for subway, bus and walking. VisitKorea calls it the most widely used online map among Koreans.
  • KakaoMap: a second map app in English. Handy when one app finds a place and the other does not.
  • k.ride: Kakao Mobility's taxi app for visitors. VisitKorea says it takes credit cards from overseas.
  • A translation app of your choice, for menus and short questions.

Set up each app and add your card at home, on hotel Wi-Fi, not at the taxi stand.

Your first-day checklist

  • Some cash in won, withdrawn at an ATM with a Global sign. Visit Seoul says these accept international cards.
  • A T-money card, loaded before you head down to the platform.
  • A plug adapter for two round holes, and a quick look at your charger for "100-240V".
  • Your passport in your bag if you plan to shop. Tax refunds need it. Our tax refund guide has the steps.
  • Your hotel address in Korean, saved as a screenshot for taxi drivers.

Where to go first

Still choosing a base? Our where to stay in Seoul guide compares five neighborhoods by subway line and airport link. If shopping is the plan, start with the Myeongdong beauty shopping route or the Seoul shopping guide by area.

item.title: Where to Stay in Seoul: 5 Neighborhoods for a First Trip
item.description: Where to stay in Seoul on a first trip: Myeongdong, Hongdae, Insadong, Gangnam and Seongsu compared by subway line, airport link and who each one suits.
item.content:encoded:
For a first trip, stay in Myeongdong for central shopping and a direct airport bus, Hongdae for cafes, nightlife and the airport train, or Insadong and Jongno for palaces and traditional streets. Gangnam suits business trips and modern Seoul, and Seongsu suits repeat visitors who want cafes and pop-ups. Pick a hotel near a subway station.

Seoul is big, and where you sleep decides how much of your trip you spend on the subway. The good news: the subway is easy, and every area below has a station close by. The real choice is about the mood you want outside your door and how far you are from the airport.

Here are five neighborhoods first-timers usually weigh, and who each one suits.

The short version

  • Myeongdong: central, busy, an easy all-rounder.
  • Hongdae: young, lively, direct airport train.
  • Insadong and Jongno: palaces, hanok and tea houses.
  • Gangnam: modern, business-friendly, south of the river.
  • Seongsu: cafes and pop-ups in old factory buildings, better for a second trip.

Myeongdong (Jung-gu): the easy, central choice

  • Who it suits: first-timers, shoppers, and anyone who wants to walk out the door into the action.
  • Subway: Line 4, Myeongdong Station, Exits 5 to 10 for the shopping streets, per Visit Seoul.
  • From the airport: limousine bus 6001 serves Myeongdong and Dongdaemun, and by train it is about 1 hour 10 minutes with a transfer to Line 4 at Seoul Station, Visit Seoul says (as of June 2026. Source: Visit Seoul).
  • Know before you book: Visit Seoul says the area fills with tourists during holiday periods. Expect crowds.
  • Plan it: our Myeongdong beauty shopping route shows how to use a half day here.

Hongdae: young, lively, and close to the airport train

  • Who it suits: solo travelers, friends, and anyone who wants cafes, street music and a late night.
  • Subway: Hongik University Station, on Line 2, the Gyeongui-Jungang Line and the Airport Railroad.
  • From the airport: about 1 hour on the AREX All-Stop train, with no transfer, per Visit Seoul. Limousine bus 6002 serves Hongdae and Jongno.
  • What it’s like: Visit Seoul describes cafes “around every corner” and street performance stages. Walk north to Yeonnam-dong for coffee, or south toward Hapjeong for handmade goods.
  • Know before you book: the streets around the station stay busy into the evening. Pick a side street if you sleep lightly.

Insadong and Jongno: palaces and tradition

  • Who it suits: history lovers, couples, and anyone who wants old Seoul within walking distance.
  • Subway: Anguk Station on Line 3, or Jongno 3-ga Station on Lines 1, 3 and 5, per Visit Seoul.
  • From the airport: limousine bus 6011 serves Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung palaces, and 6002 serves Jongno, Visit Seoul says (as of June 2026).
  • What it’s like: Visit Seoul calls Insadong a quaint neighborhood with antique shops, art galleries and traditional tea houses. On Sundays the streets close to traffic and fill with street performers. Nearby Ikseon-dong has hanok built between 1920 and 1930, now home to cafes and restaurants, Visit Seoul says.
  • Know before you book: many hotels and guesthouses here sit in small alleys. Check the walk to Anguk or Jongno 3-ga Station before you book.

Gangnam: modern Seoul, south of the river

  • Who it suits: business travelers, return visitors, and anyone headed to COEX or Garosu-gil.
  • Subway: Gangnam Station is on Line 2 and the Sinbundang Line. Sinsa Station, for Garosu-gil, is on Line 3 and the Sinbundang Line.
  • From the airport: limousine bus 6020 serves the Express Bus Terminal and Gangnam. By train, Visit Seoul estimates about 1 hour 50 minutes with a transfer to Line 2 (as of June 2026).
  • What it’s like: Visit Seoul calls the Gangnam Station area one of Seoul’s busiest transportation hubs, with a nightlife district full of restaurants, bars and clubs just north of the station.
  • Know before you book: the palaces and old markets are north of the Han River, so sightseeing days start with a longer ride.

Seongsu: cafes and pop-ups for a second trip

  • Who it suits: repeat visitors, design and fashion fans, and K-beauty shoppers who like to test before they buy.
  • Subway: Line 2, Seongsu Station. Seoul Forest Station on the Suin-Bundang Line is close by, per Visit Seoul.
  • What it’s like: “once known primarily for factories and small workshops,” Visit Seoul says, now full of cafes, design studios, fashion brands and pop-ups that change often.
  • Know before you book: it sits farther east than the other areas, so trips to the palaces take longer. Check the walk from your hotel to Seongsu Station.
  • Plan it: our Seongsu beauty shopping route lists exits and a walking order.

How to pick the exact spot

  • Walk time to the station matters most. Check it in Naver Map or KakaoMap before you book.
  • Count the lines. A station with two or three lines saves transfers every day.
  • Check the airport bus stop. If you will take a limousine bus, look up where your route stops near the hotel.
  • Light sleeper? Look one or two streets back from the main nightlife strips.

Split your stay

On a longer trip, two bases can save travel time. One option is a few nights north of the river (Myeongdong or Jongno) and a few nights in Gangnam or Seongsu. Hongdae is easy for the last night because the AREX All-Stop train stops there on the way to Incheon Airport, per Visit Seoul.

Before you land

Read our Seoul travel tips for the airport train, T-money and map apps. Shopping is part of the plan? Our Seoul shopping guide by area covers what to buy in each of these neighborhoods.

item.title: Seongsu Seoul Beauty Shopping: A Simple Half-Day Route
item.description: Seongsu, Seoul for beauty shoppers: the subway exits, Olive Young N Seongsu, AMORE Seongsu, pop-up streets and a half-day route you can save.
item.content:encoded:
Take Seoul Subway Line 2 to Seongsu Station. Olive Young N Seongsu is about 118 m from Exit 4, and AMORE Seongsu is about 264 m from Exit 2, per Visit Seoul. Then walk Yeonmujang-gil for pop-ups. Skip Mondays if you want AMORE Seongsu, which closes that day.

Seongsu-dong used to be a district of shoe factories, printing shops and auto parts suppliers, Visit Seoul says. Today the old warehouses hold cafes, flagship stores and pop-ups, and beauty is a big part of the mix. Olive Young opened Olive Young N Seongsu here in late November 2024, and CJ Newsroom called it the chain’s largest store in Korea in January 2025.

Seongsu is not where you go to fill a suitcase fast. It is where you test, compare and get your skin checked. Here is how to plan half a day.

Getting there

  • Subway: Seoul Subway Line 2, Seongsu Station. Visit Seoul lists the main stops below about 120 to 540 m from Exits 2, 3 and 4.
  • Other way in: Seoul Forest Station on the Suin-Bundang Line, listed by Visit Seoul next to D Museum and Seoul Forest park.
  • Map tip: search each store by its English name in a map app. Seongsu has several Olive Young locations, and their names sound alike.
  • Avoid Mondays if AMORE Seongsu is on your list. It is closed that day, Visit Seoul says.

What you’ll find

  • Olive Young N Seongsu: five floors and about 4,620 square meters, nearly nine times the size of an average Olive Young Town store, CJ Newsroom reported. The first floor has a pop-up zone and cafe. Floors 2 and 3 hold 12 zones such as Color Makeup and Daily Skincare. The 4th floor is for VIP members. Staff speak several languages, and shelves carry electronic English labels. Visit Seoul lists it at 13 Yeonmujang 7-gil, open daily 10:00 to 22:00, about 118 m from Exit 4.
  • AMORE Seongsu: Amorepacific’s flagship, with Sulwhasoo, Laneige, HERA, Innisfree, ETUDE, IOPE and Mamonde under one roof. You can have foundation and lipstick matched to your skin tone, and reservations are recommended for that. Visit Seoul lists it at 7 Achasan-ro 11-gil, open Tuesday to Sunday 10:30 to 20:30, about 264 m from Exit 2.
  • Olive Young Beauty Mansion Seongsu: four floors and about 1,653 square meters, opened June 30, 2026, Olive Young said. Floors 2 and 3 focus on makeup and skincare services, including 3D skin diagnostics and a Beauty Device Studio for trying K-beauty devices. Olive Young placed it to link Yeonmujang-gil with the northern part of Seongsu.
  • OLIVE BETTER Seongsu: Olive Young’s wellness store, opened Oct. 30, 2026, on four floors. It has a gua sha island, inner beauty displays and a Better Bar serving shakes and teas, Olive Young said.
  • Postes Seongsu Boutique: a fragrance shop at 77 Yeonmujang-gil, open daily 11:00 to 20:00, about 397 m from Exit 3, Visit Seoul says. You can write a note at its mailbox, and Postes mails it for free.
  • Yeonmujang-gil: the main street for murals, shopfronts and seasonal pop-ups. Visit Seoul lists it as open 24 hours.

A sample route

  1. AMORE Seongsu (from Exit 2). Go first, when it opens at 10:30, if you booked a custom shade.
  2. Olive Young N Seongsu (near Exit 4). Check the first-floor pop-up, then shop floors 2 and 3. Our first Olive Young list keeps the basket short.
  3. Yeonmujang-gil. Walk slowly. Visit Seoul notes that walls and storefronts change with brand collaborations, so look down side streets.
  4. Postes Seongsu Boutique. A quiet stop for fragrance after the crowds.
  5. Beauty Mansion or OLIVE BETTER. Pick one, based on whether you want skin services or wellness snacks. Search the name in your map app for the route.
  6. Seoul Forest. End at the park if you have time, then take the Suin-Bundang Line from Seoul Forest Station.

Before you go

  • Book services early. Olive Young N Seongsu releases lesson slots every Friday at noon for the following week, Visit Seoul says.
  • Wear walking shoes. Stops are spread out, and the side streets are worth a look.
  • Save receipts together for tax refunds at the airport.
  • Check hours on the day. Pop-ups and store hours change often in Seongsu.

Pop-ups: how to find this week's

  • Expect change. Visit Seoul describes Seongsu as a place where a new concept store replaces yesterday's pop-up. Any list goes out of date fast.
  • Check the big stores first. Olive Young N Seongsu has a pop-up zone on its first floor, and Beauty Mansion has pop-up and shop-in-shop spaces on its first floor, Olive Young says.
  • Search the night before. Brands announce pop-ups on their own Instagram accounts. Search "Seongsu pop-up" with the date, then save the address in your map app.

Tax refunds in Seongsu

  • Bring your passport. Stores check it at the register.
  • Know the minimum. A refund needs ₩15,000 or more per purchase, and an immediate refund at the register works for single payments under ₩1,000,000, up to ₩5,000,000 for the trip (as of Nov. 17, 2026. Source: VisitKorea. Rules can change, so check at the counter).
  • Keep it sealed. Refunded items must stay new and unopened until you leave Korea (as of Nov. 17, 2026. Source: VisitKorea).

Airport steps and how much you get back are in our tax refund guide.

Seongsu or Myeongdong?

  • Seongsu suits trying things: skin and scalp scans, makeup lessons, custom shades and pop-ups.
  • Myeongdong suits stocking up: many Olive Young branches, Daiso and brand shops on a few streets. See our Myeongdong route.
  • Doing both? Our Seoul shopping guide compares the main areas.

item.title: Seoul Shopping Guide: Where to Buy K-Beauty by Area
item.description: A Seoul shopping guide for beauty: what Myeongdong, Hongdae, Seongsu, Gangnam and Insadong are each good for, the subway stops, and tax refund basics.
item.content:encoded:
For K-beauty in Seoul, go to Myeongdong to stock up, Seongsu to test products and get skin checked, Hongdae for trendy shops near the airport train, Garosu-gil in Gangnam for brand flagships, and Insadong for traditional gifts. Bring your passport: purchases of ₩15,000 or more can qualify for a tax refund (as of Nov. 17, 2026, per VisitKorea).

Seoul has more beauty stores than most visitors can cover in one trip. The trick is to match each area to what you want: a big haul, a skin check, a brand flagship or a gift. Visit Seoul’s own shopping course sends visitors to Myeongdong for K-beauty and to Insadong for traditional crafts, and the other areas fill the gaps.

Here is what each area is for, how to get there, and what to know before you pay.

Myeongdong: the big haul

  • Good for: stocking up in one walk. Visit Seoul says the area has many Korean cosmetics stores with competitive prices.
  • Getting there: Subway Line 4, Myeongdong Station, Exits 5 to 10, per Visit Seoul.
  • Hours: open daily, but hours vary by store, Visit Seoul says.
  • Expect: crowds, street food stalls and several branches of the same chains. Search each store by name in a map app.
  • Plan it: our Myeongdong beauty shopping route gives a half-day order, from Daiso to Olive Young.

Seongsu: test, compare, get scanned

  • Good for: trying products and booking services such as skin scans and makeup lessons.
  • Getting there: Subway Line 2, Seongsu Station. Olive Young N Seongsu is about 118 m from Exit 4, Visit Seoul says.
  • Big stops: Olive Young N Seongsu, about 4,620 square meters over five floors, which CJ Newsroom called the chain’s largest store in Korea in January 2025. AMORE Seongsu, Amorepacific’s flagship, matches foundation and lipstick to your skin tone and is closed on Mondays, per Visit Seoul.
  • Expect: pop-ups that change from week to week.
  • Plan it: our Seongsu beauty shopping route has exits, hours and a walking order.

Hongdae: trendy and close to the airport train

  • Good for: fashion and cosmetics in one area, with a younger crowd. Visit Seoul describes Hongdae R3 Fashion Street as densely packed with clothing and cosmetic stores.
  • Getting there: Hongik University Station, on Subway Line 2, the Gyeongui-Jungang Line and the Airport Railroad. R3 Fashion Street is about 350 m from Exit 9, Visit Seoul says.
  • Big stop: Olive Young Hongdae Town, which CJ Newsroom lists as one of the brand’s regional flagships.
  • Expect: street performers nearby. Visit Seoul lists a busking street close to Exit 8.

Gangnam (Garosu-gil): flagships and makeup artists

  • Good for: brand flagships and a slower, boutique pace. Visit Seoul says Garosu-gil in Sinsa-dong has a variety of fashion stores, character shops and cafes.
  • Getting there: Sinsa Station, on Subway Line 3 and the Sinbundang Line, Exit 8.
  • Beauty stop: Jung Saem Mool Plops, the flagship of Korean makeup artist Jung Saem Mool, with brand showcases and beauty classes. Visit Seoul lists it at 51-1 Garosu-gil, open daily 11:00 to 21:00, about 638 m from Exit 8.
  • A bit of history: Olive Young opened its first store in Sinsa-dong in 1999, CJ Newsroom says.

Insadong: gifts, not skincare

  • Good for: traditional souvenirs. Visit Seoul calls it one of the best places in Seoul to buy traditional Korean art and souvenirs, with handicraft, pottery and stationery shops.
  • Getting there: Anguk Station on Subway Line 3. Visit Seoul pages give both Exit 5 and Exit 6, so check your map app.
  • Skip it for skincare. Visit Seoul’s Insadong page does not describe it as a cosmetics area. Pair it with Myeongdong instead.

If you only have one day

  1. Morning in Seongsu for scans and testing, especially if you booked a service.
  2. Afternoon in Myeongdong to buy what you liked.
  3. Evening back at the hotel sorting tax refund receipts into one envelope.

Tax refund basics

  • Minimum: ₩15,000 or more per purchase at a store with a Tax Refund sign (as of Nov. 17, 2026. Source: VisitKorea).
  • At the register: an immediate refund works for single payments under ₩1,000,000, and no more than ₩5,000,000 for the whole trip (as of Nov. 17, 2026. Source: VisitKorea).
  • Who qualifies: visitors staying in Korea less than six months. Items must be new and unopened, and you must leave Korea within three months of buying them (as of Nov. 17, 2026. Source: VisitKorea).
  • Passport: bring the original every time you shop.

Rules can change, so check at the counter. Airport steps are in our tax refund guide.

Plan your days

  • Group by line. Hongdae and Seongsu are both on Line 2. Myeongdong is on Line 4. Sinsa and Anguk are both on Line 3.
  • Mind Mondays. AMORE Seongsu closes on Mondays, Visit Seoul says.
  • Go to Insadong on Sunday if you like street performers. Visit Seoul says the streets close to traffic that day.
  • Buy heavy things last. Creams and sheet masks add up. Shop the big stores near the end of your trip.

Make a short list first

Big stores carry thousands of products. Decide on a few before you walk in.

  • First trip to Olive Young? Start with our first Olive Young list.
  • Buying for others? Our Korea beauty gift list sorts gifts by who they are for.
  • Low budget? Our Daiso guide covers beauty basics at Daiso prices.

item.title: Korean Brows: How to Get the Straight, Natural Brow Look
item.description: How to do Korean brows: the straight, soft shape, brow pencil vs. brow mascara, how to fill step by step, shade words to know, and budget brow picks at Daiso.
item.content:encoded:
Korean brows are usually straighter and softer than a high, sharp arch. Fill the lower edge in a level line with a slim pencil, keep the front light and brush it upward, then set the hairs with a tinted brow mascara. Daiso stocks both brow pencils and brow mascaras, so a basic kit costs little.

Brows change how a whole face reads. The Korean brow look is a good place to start if your brows feel too sharp, too thin or too drawn on.

It is soft, fairly straight and close to your natural shape. You need two low-cost products and a few minutes.

What makes a brow look Korean

  • A straighter line. The brow stays fairly level from front to tail, with a small lift near the end. Koreans call it 일자 눈썹 (straight brows).
  • A soft front. The inner part is light and brushed up, not filled in as a solid block.
  • A gentle color. Often your hair color or a step lighter. Soft brown and taupe shades are easy to find on Korean shelves.
  • Hairs you can see. The finish looks like brushed brow hair, not a painted shape.

Brow pencil or brow mascara

  • Brow pencil: fills gaps and draws the shape. Korean brow pencils are often slim, twist-up auto pencils (오토펜슬), so you get thin strokes without a sharpener.
  • Flat or angled pencil: a wider tip for faster filling. Good if your brows are sparse.
  • Brow mascara (브로우카라): a tinted gel on a small wand. It colors the hairs and holds them in place.
  • Both: pencil for the shape, then brow mascara on top. This is an easy way to wear the look every day.

Who should buy what

  • Sparse or short brows: a slim pencil first. Add brow mascara later if you want.
  • Full brows that look heavy: a light brown brow mascara alone. It softens dark hairs.
  • Brows that won’t stay put: a brow mascara labeled fixing (픽싱) to hold them up.
  • Hot days or long walks: a pencil tagged waterproof (워터프루프).
  • First try: one slim pencil. You can add the rest once you like the shape.

Daiso picks

These were on Daiso Mall on Nov. 17, 2026. Stock and prices change, so check the shelf or Daiso Mall before you go.

Brow pencils

  • Tag Slim Brow Pencil. A slim auto pencil in 2호 Ash Brown (ash brown) and 1호 Dark Brown (dark brown).
  • The Bom Skinny Brow Pencil. A dual-type slim pencil in shades like 04 Taupe Beige.
  • Holika Holika Softune Angled Edge Eyebrow. An angled tip for wider strokes, in shades like 02 Soft Beige.
  • Bonsep Waterproof Flat Eyebrow. A flat, waterproof pencil in shades like 01 Taupe Gray.

Brow mascaras

  • Tag Air Fixing Brow Cara, 9 g. Light brown and dark brown.
  • Bonsep Slim Fixing Browcara. A slim wand in 01 Gray Brown and 02 Natural Brown.
  • Play 101 by Etude Soft Browcara. Three shades: 01 Pink Brown, 02 Taupe Gray and 03 Natural Brown.

Tools

  • Straight eyebrow razor, 2 pack. For tidying stray hairs under the brow.
  • KAI T-shaped mini eyebrow razor, 3 pack. A small T-shaped razor for tidying around the brow.

A pencil and a brow mascara from this list make a basic brow kit. Our budget makeup guide builds a full kit around them.

Tidy before you fill

  • Brush first, then trim. Brush hairs up and trim only what sticks far above the line.
  • Shave below, not above. Remove strays under the brow to make the lower line look straight. Leave the top edge alone.
  • Go slowly. Take a little at a time and check in the mirror from arm’s length.

Make the brows match the rest

Soft brows suit the rest of the Korean makeup look: a thin cushion base and a gradient lip tint. If your hair is dyed lighter, pick a brow shade close to your new hair, not your roots. For more aisles to shop, see our Daiso beauty guide.

How to fill Korean brows, step by step

  1. Brush up. Comb the hairs up and out with a spoolie so you see the real shape.
  2. Draw the lower line. With a slim pencil, draw short strokes along the bottom edge, from below the arch to the tail. Keep it level, not curved down.
  3. Fill the gaps. Short, light strokes in the direction the hairs grow.
  4. Keep the front soft. Use what is left on the pencil, or skip it. Brush the front hairs straight up.
  5. Set it. One coat of brow mascara, brushed up at the front and along the hairs at the tail.
  6. Blend. Run a clean spoolie through once so no line looks drawn on.

Shopping for brows in Seoul

Daiso first. Brow pencils, brow mascaras and brow razors all sit in the eye makeup and tool aisles. Daiso puts the shade in brackets, like [02 내추럴브라운]. Screenshot it so you grab the same one.

Olive Young for testers. Olive Young carries more brow brands and shades. Use the testers before you pick a shade. Our Olive Young list covers how the store works.

Brow mascara is called 브로우카라. Search that word on Daiso Mall or show it to staff.

Safety notes

  • Skip DIY tints. The FDA warns that permanent eyelash and eyebrow tints and dyes have been known to cause serious eye injuries, including blindness. A tinted brow mascara washes off and is not the same thing.
  • Use clean testers. The FDA says testers carry a higher risk of contamination. Swatch on your hand, or use a clean cotton swab.
  • Don't share. The FDA says not to share or swap eye cosmetics.
  • Stop if your eyes are sore. The FDA advises not using eye cosmetics if you have an eye infection or the skin around the eye is inflamed.

item.title: Korean Double Cleansing: Oil or Balm, Then Foam
item.description: How Korean double cleansing works, who needs a cleansing oil or balm first, how to make it turn milky with water, and when one gentle wash is enough.
item.content:encoded:
Korean double cleansing means a cleansing oil or balm first, then a water-based cleanser such as a foam. Cleveland Clinic dermatologists say it helps if you wear makeup or waterproof sunscreen, and most people without makeup do fine with one gentle wash. Massage the oil onto dry skin, add a little water until it turns milky, then rinse.

Double cleansing is the first step of many Korean night routines. It sounds like extra work. On most nights, it is only one more minute at the sink.

It is also optional. Here is who it helps, how to do it so the oil rinses clean, and when one wash is enough.

What double cleansing means

“Double cleansing means cleansing your face twice, first with an oil-based product and then followed by a water-based cleanser,” Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Jane Wu, MD, explains.

  • Step 1, oil or balm: loosens oil-based things on your skin, such as makeup, sunscreen and sebum, Dr. Wu says.
  • Step 2, water-based cleanser: usually a foam. It washes away water-based things such as sweat and dirt.

Who it helps, and who can skip it

  • You wear makeup: Cleveland Clinic dermatologist Kathryn Anderson, MD, suggests double cleansing for people who wear makeup.
  • You wear waterproof makeup or waterproof sunscreen: this is where the oil step helps most, Dr. Wu says.
  • Oily skin: Dr. Wu says an oil cleanser can help remove excess oil as a first step.
  • No makeup: Dr. Anderson does not recommend it. It can overcomplicate your routine and be more drying.
  • Dry or sensitive skin: keep it for nights you really need it. Dermatologists worry more about overwashing than about skipping a step, Dr. Wu says.

Want to know how sunscreen labels work first? Read our Korean sunscreen guide.

Oil or balm?

  • Cleansing oil: a liquid, usually in a pump bottle. Round Lab, for one, sells its 1025 Dokdo Cleansing Oil for all skin types.
  • Cleansing balm: a solid you scoop out, which softens as you massage it in. Banila Co sells its Clean it Zero Original balm in a 180 ml jar and in a travel kit of sixteen 3 ml minis on its official Korean store (checked Nov. 17, 2026). The minis are easy to pack for a trip.

Both do the same job. Pick the texture you like using.

How to emulsify a cleansing oil

Emulsifying means adding water so the oil turns milky and rinses away. Round Lab gives these steps:

  1. Start dry. Use completely dry hands on a completely dry face. Water starts the milky change too early, Round Lab says.
  2. Use one to two pumps.
  3. Massage for 30 to 60 seconds in gentle circles. Spend extra time on the forehead, nose and jawline.
  4. Add a little lukewarm water. Wet your hands and keep massaging. The oil turns from clear or golden to white and milky.
  5. Keep going 15 to 20 seconds.
  6. Rinse until the milkiness is gone. Your skin should feel clean, not tight or slippery.

The second cleanse

  1. Stay damp. Dr. Wu suggests skipping the towel between steps.
  2. Use your fingertips. The AAD says a washcloth or sponge can irritate your skin.
  3. Massage gently. Do not scrub, the AAD says.
  4. Rinse with lukewarm water. Water that is too hot can dry out skin, Dr. Wu says.
  5. Pat dry with a soft towel, then go on with your skincare steps.

Pick the second cleanser by skin type

These are Dr. Wu’s suggestions:

  • Dry, sensitive: a gentle, unscented water-based cleanser. Cream cleansers are less drying than foams.
  • Oily, acne-prone: a water-based foaming cleanser.
  • Combination: a water-based foaming cleanser.
  • Normal: a gentle, unscented cleanser. Cream or foam is up to you.

She also suggests avoiding harsh, very drying or fragranced cleansers for every skin type.

Common mistakes

  • Oil on a wet face. Round Lab says to start dry.
  • Rushing the massage. Give it the full 30 to 60 seconds.
  • Hot water. Use lukewarm.
  • Leaving residue. Round Lab says leftover oil can trap debris. Rinse until no milkiness is left.
  • Oil cleansing every morning. Round Lab calls it a night step.

Finished cleansing on a mask night? Our sheet mask guide covers what comes next.

Morning vs. night

  • Night with makeup or sunscreen: cleansing oil or balm, then a water-based cleanser.
  • Night without makeup: one gentle cleanser is enough, Cleveland Clinic's dermatologist says.
  • Morning: one gentle wash. Round Lab says mornings usually do not need oil cleansing.
  • After a workout: the AAD says to wash as soon as possible after sweating.

If your skin feels tight afterward

  • Cut back. Cleveland Clinic's dermatologist worries more about overwashing than about skipping a step. Overwashing can lead to dryness and irritation, she says.
  • Switch your second step. For dry or sensitive skin, she suggests a gentle, unscented cleanser. Cream cleansers are less drying than foams.
  • Try micellar water. Using micellar water to remove makeup before one water-based cleanser is an alternative to double cleansing, she says.
  • Moisturize. The AAD suggests moisturizer if your skin feels dry or itchy. See our dry skin routine.

Korean words on the shelf

  • 클렌징 오일 (keul-len-jing o-il): cleansing oil.
  • 클렌징 밤 (keul-len-jing bam): cleansing balm.
  • 폼 클렌저 (pom keul-len-jeo): foam cleanser.
  • 클렌징 (keul-len-jing): cleansing, the shelf name for the whole step.

Shopping for one step? Show the word to a staff member.

item.title: Korean Pimple Patch Guide: How to Use Acne Patches
item.description: What a Korean pimple patch can and can't do, hydrocolloid vs. microneedle patches, how to put one on, how labels differ in Korea and the US, and Daiso picks.
item.content:encoded:
A Korean pimple patch is a small sticker you put on a spot. Plain hydrocolloid patches cover a pimple that has a head or has opened, soak up fluid and keep your fingers off it. They don't reach deep, painful bumps. If breakouts keep coming back, see a board-certified dermatologist.

Pimple patches are one of the easiest Korean skincare buys to bring home. They are small, cheap and quick to use. In Seoul you’ll find them at Daiso, Olive Young and many pharmacies.

They are also easy to expect too much from. A patch covers a spot. It does not clear acne. Here is what a patch can do, which kind to pick and how to read the box.

What a pimple patch does

Most basic patches are made of hydrocolloid. The Korea Pharmaceutical Information Center describes hydrocolloid as a mix of gelatin, carboxymethylcellulose and pectin that turns into a gel as it takes up fluid.

On a pimple, that means three things:

  • It soaks up fluid from a spot that has a head or has opened. That is why the patch turns white.
  • It keeps your fingers off. The AAD says picking and popping make acne take longer to clear and raise your risk of scars and dark spots.
  • It hides the spot a little. Thin, clear patches sit flat under a mask or a hat.

What it doesn’t do

  • It won’t reach deep bumps. An AAD press release quotes dermatologist Fatima Fahs, MD: pimple patches “help draw out fluid from pimples and stop you from picking, but they won’t work on deep acne.”
  • It won’t stop new spots. For acne that keeps coming back, the AAD says to partner with a board-certified dermatologist.
  • It isn’t for an infected spot. The Korea Pharmaceutical Information Center says hydrocolloid dressings should not be used on infected wounds. If a spot is hot, swollen or getting worse, see a doctor.

Who should buy what

  • You pick at spots: plain hydrocolloid patches in a mixed-size pack.
  • You want to wear one in the day: a thin, clear patch. Look for 베벨링 (beveling) on the box, which means a tapered edge.
  • You want something fun for a weekend: printed patches, like the heart and star shapes at Daiso.
  • You have a small bump with no head: some people try a microneedle-style patch. Read the box for what the brand says it does, and remember a patch won’t reach deep bumps.

How to put one on

  1. Wash your hands and the spot. Pat it fully dry. Patches don’t stick to wet or oily skin.
  2. Pick a patch bigger than the spot. The edge should sit on clear skin.
  3. Press it on before skincare. Put the patch on clean skin, then apply your other products around it.
  4. Leave it on for the time on the box. Some boxes say overnight is fine.
  5. Peel it off slowly from the edge. Change it when it turns white and puffy.

If your skin turns red or itchy under the patch, stop using it.

Daiso picks

These were on Daiso Mall on Nov. 17, 2026. Names, counts and categories are from Daiso Mall, and stock changes.

  • Withderm Skin Cover, 44 patches. Listed under household medical supplies. A 105-patch value pack is also sold.
  • Withderm Beveling Type, 15 or 33 patches. The beveled edge is the thin, tapered rim.
  • Madeca21 Relief Spot Care Patch, 68 patches. Listed under skincare spot care.
  • Mimorang Micro Trouble Patch, small, 10 patches. A microneedle-style patch listed under skincare. Daiso Mall tags it with panthenol, madecassoside and hyaluronic acid.
  • OOTD Lab Heart or Star Spot Patch, 24 patches. Printed shapes, listed under household medical supplies.

Not every Daiso store has every patch. Daiso Mall’s store finder (매장 상품 찾기) shows which branches have stock. Our Daiso beauty guide has more of the beauty aisle.

At a pharmacy

Korean pharmacies sell patches next to acne creams and ointments. Some of those creams are medicines. Ask the pharmacist before you buy them, as we explain in our Korean pharmacy guide.

Fit patches into your routine

A patch is one small step. Keep the rest simple: a gentle cleanser, a moisturizer and sunscreen in the morning. The AAD says to give any acne treatment time to work, since it may take several weeks to a few months to see a difference. Our Korean skincare steps guide shows where each step goes, and our cica guide explains the centella names you’ll see on spot care shelves.

Hydrocolloid or microneedle: which patch for which spot

  • A whitehead or a spot that has opened: a plain hydrocolloid patch. It covers the spot and soaks up fluid.
  • A small bump with no head yet: many Korean brands sell microneedle or "micro" patches for this, often with skincare ingredients. Read the box for what the brand says it does.
  • A deep, sore bump under the skin: a patch won't reach it. The AAD notes that pimple patches won't work on deep acne.
  • Lots of spots at once, or spots that leave marks: see a dermatologist rather than buying more patches.

How to read the box in Korea

Look for one of three words. 의료기기 (medical device), 의약외품 (quasi-drug) or 화장품 (cosmetic). The word tells you how the product is regulated in Korea.

Why it matters. The Korea Pharmaceutical Information Center says Korea's drug regulator manages wound dressings (창상피복재) as medical devices, while bandages and plasters are quasi-drugs. A Korean Ministry of Food and Drug Safety answer says a patch meant to protect and care for skin with acne does not fit the definition of a cosmetic.

Where you'll see them. Daiso Mall lists some patches under household medical supplies (가정의료용품) and others under skincare spot care (스팟케어).

Before you pack them for home

  • US rules are different. The FDA says whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug depends on its intended use. A product made to treat acne is regulated as a drug.
  • Salicylic acid patches. The FDA's OTC acne monograph (M006, final order posted Nov. 23, 2021) lists salicylic acid at 0.5 to 2 percent as an acne active ingredient. US versions carry a Drug Facts label.
  • Plain patches pack flat. A sheet of patches weighs almost nothing and fits in a passport cover.

item.title: Korean Sheet Masks: Types, Timing and Where to Buy
item.description: Cotton, hydrogel and bio-cellulose sheet masks explained, how long to leave one on, how often to use it, and where to buy masks for less in Seoul.
item.content:encoded:
A Korean sheet mask is a single-use sheet soaked in essence. Most boxes say to leave it on 15 to 20 minutes, a 2022 study in Scientific Reports found, and its authors advise staying under 20. Fiber sheets are the most common, hydrogel is a jelly-like gel, and Daiso in Seoul is a low-cost place to buy them.

A sheet mask is the easiest K-beauty souvenir to try. It is one sheet, one pouch, one evening. In Seoul you can pick one up cheaply at Daiso.

The choice is the hard part. Stores sell cotton sheets, jelly-like gels and thin bio-cellulose masks side by side. Here is what each one is, how long to wear it, and where to buy it for less.

What a sheet mask does

A sheet mask holds a watery essence against your face for a few minutes. A Cleveland Clinic dermatologist says sheet masks tend to feel more hydrating than cream masks, because the sheet spreads the moisturizer right where it sits.

She also says the effect is temporary. So think of a mask as a boost before a big day, not a fix.

The three main types

  • Cotton or fiber sheet: the classic. A soft fabric sheet soaked in essence. Some use plant fibers: the Vaseline masks at Daiso use a eucalyptus-fiber sheet, Daiso Mall says. This is the type you will see most, and often the least expensive.
  • Hydrogel: a jelly-like gel sheet instead of fabric. Researchers describe hydrogels as flexible materials made to stick to skin (Polymers, 2025). Some hydrogel masks are meant to stay on for hours, like the one in our first Olive Young list. Always read the box.
  • Bio-cellulose: a sheet made from cellulose that certain bacteria produce, a 2020 paper in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology explains. It is a different material from plant cotton, though you use it the same way.

How long to leave it on

  • Most boxes say 15 to 20 minutes. That is what most sheet masks recommend, a 2022 study in Scientific Reports found.
  • Stay under 20 minutes. In that study, exposure to preservatives rose sharply once masks stayed on 25 minutes or longer. The authors think water evaporating from the sheet concentrates what is left in it. They advise under 20 minutes.
  • Some say less. On Daiso Mall, the VT PDRN Glow Sheet Mask says 10 to 20 minutes and the Vaseline masks say about 10.
  • Hydrogel can differ. Follow the box, not a general rule.

How often to use one

No official rule exists. Cleveland Clinic’s dermatologist puts cleansing, daily sunscreen and moisturizer first, and calls a mask a complement to them.

  • Use it when you want a boost, such as the night before a photo day or after a long flight.
  • New to a mask? The American Academy of Dermatology suggests testing a new product on a small patch of skin first. Stop if your skin turns red, itchy or swollen.
  • Sensitive skin: Cleveland Clinic’s dermatologist suggests looking for fragrance-free and dye-free labels.

How to use a sheet mask

  1. Cleanse first. Wash with a gentle cleanser to remove makeup and dirt, Cleveland Clinic advises. Our double cleansing guide covers nights with makeup or sunscreen.
  2. Unfold and line it up. Match the eye, nose and mouth holes, then smooth the sheet out from the center.
  3. Set a timer. Use the time on the box.
  4. Pat in what is left. Daiso’s directions say to peel it off and pat in the leftover essence, with no rinsing.
  5. Finish your routine. Moisturizer goes after the mask. See where it fits in our Korean skincare steps.

Pick a mask by how your skin feels

  • Dry or tight: Cleveland Clinic suggests looking for hyaluronic acid on the label. Our dry skin routine has more.
  • Just want hydration: a cotton or fiber sheet with a watery essence is the simple start.
  • Want a longer, quieter night: try a hydrogel and read its wear time.

Where to buy sheet masks for less in Seoul

  • Daiso: Daiso keeps fixed prices of ₩5,000 or less, BizWatch reported in July 2025. The VT PDRN Glow Sheet Mask and the two Vaseline sheet masks were listed on Daiso Mall (checked Nov. 16, 2026. Source: Daiso Mall). See them all in our Daiso Korea guide.
  • Olive Young Central Myeongdong Town: its "Mask Library" is a large mask section sorted by skin type and concern, Cosinkorea reported in March 2026. Go here for choice, Daiso for price.
  • Buy a few kinds first. Try one cotton and one hydrogel before you buy a whole box of either.

Packing masks for the flight home

  • Carry-on (US flights): TSA allows liquids and gels in containers of 3.4 oz (100 ml) or less, all in one quart-size bag (as of Nov. 16, 2026. Source: TSA. Rules can change, so check before you fly.)
  • Pouch size: the Daiso masks above hold 23 to 25 ml each, under the limit. A stack still fills a quart bag fast.
  • Pack them flat in your checked bag, between clothes, so the pouches do not bend open.

Korean words on the box

  • 마스크팩 (ma-seu-keu-paek): mask pack, the everyday word for a sheet mask.
  • 시트 마스크 (si-teu ma-seu-keu): sheet mask.
  • 하이드로겔 (ha-i-deu-ro-gel): hydrogel.
  • 바이오셀룰로오스 (ba-i-o-sel-lul-lo-o-seu): bio-cellulose.
  • 보습 (bo-seup): moisturizing.

Looking for one type? Show this list to a staff member and point to the word.

item.title: Glass Skin Routine: What It Means and How to Build One
item.description: What glass skin really means, a realistic Korean routine for that hydrated look, and which product types do what, from toner to sunscreen.
item.content:encoded:
Glass skin is a Korean beauty look of smooth, clear skin so well hydrated it seems to reflect light. The American Academy of Dermatology describes the routine as a gentle cleanser, a hydrating serum, a moisturizer, gentle exfoliation and daily sunscreen, and warns that piling on products can lead to clogged pores and irritation.

“Glass skin” is a Korean beauty term for skin that looks smooth, clear and so hydrated it seems to reflect light. In Korea you will also hear 물광 (mul-gwang), “water glow.”

It is a look, not a skin type. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) says the glass-skin look might not be realistic for everyone. Pores and texture are normal. A brighter, more hydrated finish is the part most people can get closer to.

What makes skin look “glassy”

  • Water in the top layer. Hydrated skin looks smoother and catches more light. This is the part a routine can help with.
  • Less irritation. The AAD says pores tend to look more noticeable when skin is inflamed, and that hot water and scrubbing can irritate it. Gentle wins over strong.
  • Light and makeup. Much of what you see in photos is ring lights, filters and dewy makeup. Check your skin in daylight, not against a screen.

The routine, as the AAD describes it

The AAD lists five parts: a gentle cleanser, a hydrating serum, a moisturizer, exfoliation and sunscreen. Here is how each one maps onto Korean product types.

  • Gentle cleanser: morning and night, with lukewarm water. At night, many Korean routines start with an oil cleanser if you wore sunscreen or makeup. Our Korean skincare steps guide has the full order.
  • Hydrating toner (토너): in K-beauty, toner is a watery hydrating layer, not an astringent. Pat it on right after cleansing. Two or three thin layers can stand in for an essence.
  • Hydrating serum or essence (에센스, 앰플): one watery product with humectants such as glycerin or sodium hyaluronate (a form of hyaluronic acid). Cleveland Clinic suggests one serum at a time.
  • Moisturizer (크림 or 젤 크림): this holds the water in. Dry skin can go rich. Oily skin can pick a lotion or gel.
  • Sunscreen (morning): the AAD recommends a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher. Korean tubes list SPF and PA, and our Korean sunscreen guide explains both.
  • Exfoliation (now and then): an optional, gentle step. More on that below.

A realistic week

  • Every morning: cleanser, hydrating toner, moisturizer, sunscreen.
  • Every night: cleanser (oil cleanser first if you wore makeup or sunscreen), hydrating toner, serum, moisturizer.
  • Once in a while: a gentle exfoliating step. The AAD says the more aggressive the method, the less often you should use it.

That is four to five products a day. You do not need ten.

Exfoliate gently, or skip it

  • Pick the mild option. The AAD says dry, sensitive or acne-prone skin may do better with a washcloth and a mild chemical exfoliator.
  • Darker skin tones: the AAD advises avoiding strong chemical or mechanical exfoliation, because aggressive exfoliating can leave darker spots.
  • Moisturize right after. Exfoliating can dry your skin, the AAD notes.
  • Check what else you use. Retinoids, retinol and benzoyl peroxide can make skin more sensitive, the AAD says, and exfoliating on top may cause dryness or breakouts. If a doctor gave you one, ask them first.
  • Never on sunburn or on cuts and broken skin.

One example: a watery toner

Round Lab’s 1025 Dokdo Toner is one toner sold for this kind of layering. Round Lab describes it as a watery, refreshing toner that also “gently exfoliates,” and lists it as good for sensitive and all skin types. Its ingredient list starts with water, butylene glycol and glycerin, and includes protease, an enzyme (Round Lab US store, checked Nov. 17, 2026).

  • How Round Lab says to use it: after cleansing, soak a cotton pad and swipe it over your face. For a leave-on layer, leave soaked pads on for 5 to 10 minutes.
  • Where to buy: Round Lab’s official US online store.

Because it has a gentle exfoliating role, do not stack it with another exfoliating product on the same night.

Signs you are overdoing it

The AAD warns that using too many products can lead to clogged pores, irritation and breakouts. Watch for:

  • Stinging or redness after a new step.
  • New bumps where you layer the most.
  • Tight skin even after moisturizer.

Drop the newest product first. If irritation does not settle, see a dermatologist.

Glass skin words in a Korean store

  • 유리알 피부 (yu-ri-al pi-bu): glass skin, word for word.
  • 물광 (mul-gwang): water glow, the dewy finish people mean by glass skin.
  • 촉촉 (chok-chok): moist, dewy. You will see it on toners and creams.
  • 수분 (su-bun): hydration.
  • 토너, 에센스, 크림 (to-neo, e-sen-seu, keu-rim): toner, essence, cream.

Looking for one step? Show the word to a staff member.

Glass skin by skin type

  • Dry skin: keep the watery layers and finish with a rich cream. See our dry skin routine.
  • Oily skin: keep the watery layers and finish with a light, oil-free lotion or gel. See our oily skin routine.
  • Sensitive skin: skip exfoliation at first and add new products one at a time. The AAD suggests testing a new product on a small patch of skin first.

Before you buy in Seoul

  • Shop by step. Decide which step you want to add, such as a toner, then compare only toners.
  • Read the first ingredients. Hydrating products often list glycerin, butylene glycol or sodium hyaluronate near the top.
  • Want the glow today? A dewy cushion foundation gives the look on top of skincare. See our cushion guide.

item.title: Korean Skincare Routine for Oily Skin, Morning and Night
item.description: A Korean skincare routine for oily skin that keeps hydration and drops heaviness: gentle cleanser, watery toner, light lotion, sunscreen and BHA used with care.
item.content:encoded:
A Korean skincare routine for oily skin keeps the hydration and drops the heaviness: a gentle foaming cleanser, a watery toner, a light oil-free lotion or gel, and sunscreen in the morning. Dermatologists at the AAD say oily skin still needs moisturizer, and that a harsh face wash can irritate skin and trigger more oil.

Oily skin tempts you to skip moisturizer and grab the strongest face wash. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) says both are mistakes. A harsh cleanser can irritate your skin and trigger more oil, and oily skin still needs hydration.

Korean skincare suits oily skin because it leans on light, watery layers. You keep the hydration and leave out the heavy cream.

First, oily or combination?

Cleveland Clinic suggests a simple check. Wash and dry your face, wait about 30 minutes, then notice how it feels.

  • Oily all over: oily skin.
  • Oily on the forehead, nose and chin, dry on the cheeks: combination skin. See the split routine below.
  • Your type can change. Cleveland Clinic says season, hormones, stress and medications can all shift it, so check again when you travel.

Morning routine

  1. Gentle foaming cleanser. The AAD recommends a mild foaming face wash, up to twice a day and after sweating. Do not scrub.
  2. Watery toner (optional). A hydrating toner adds water with no oil. Pat it on with your hands.
  3. Light moisturizer. Pick a lotion or gel labeled oil free and noncomedogenic. The AAD says these labels mean the product is made not to clog pores.
  4. Sunscreen. The AAD recommends broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher. To avoid breakouts, it suggests sunscreens with zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, without fragrance or oils. Our Korean sunscreen guide explains SPF and PA.

Night routine

  1. Take off makeup and sunscreen. The AAD says never sleep in makeup.
  2. Gentle foaming cleanser.
  3. Watery toner.
  4. BHA, 2 to 3 nights a week (optional). More on this below.
  5. Light moisturizer.

About the oil cleanser

Many Korean routines start the night with an oil cleanser. For oily skin, the AAD advises against oil-based and alcohol-based cleansers, saying they can irritate skin. If you still want to try Korean double cleansing, test it on a small area first and stop if you break out. A gentle foaming cleanser used twice is a simpler choice.

Korean product types that suit oily skin

  • Gel cream (젤 크림): a watery, light moisturizer that sits under sunscreen without a heavy layer.
  • Lotion (로션): thinner than a cream. A good daily moisturizer for oily skin.
  • BHA toner or liquid: made with salicylic acid or betaine salicylate. The AAD says salicylic acid can help reduce oiliness, but may be too harsh for some skin.
  • Blotting paper (기름종이): the AAD suggests pressing a sheet on your face for a few seconds. Do not rub, or you spread the oil.
  • Matte makeup: the AAD suggests oil-free, water-based makeup, and products labeled matte to cut shine.

Two examples from COSRX

Both are on COSRX’s official US store (checked Nov. 17, 2026).

  • BHA Blackhead Power Liquid (100 ml): COSRX lists it for oily skin and T-zone care. The ingredient list starts with willow bark water, butylene glycol, betaine salicylate and niacinamide. COSRX recommends it 2 to 3 times a week at first, then building up. It says to wear sunscreen if you use it in the daytime, not to use it with other acids such as AHAs, BHAs, retinols and vitamin C, and that sensitive skin may get irritated.
  • Oil-Free Ultra-Moisturizing Lotion with Birch Sap (100 ml): COSRX calls it a weightless lotion and lists it for oily and combination skin. Birch sap is the first ingredient, with glycerin and sodium hyaluronate for hydration. COSRX says fragrance ingredients were removed when it was reformulated. Use it after toner and before sunscreen.

Habits that help shine

  • Hands off. The AAD says touching your face spreads oil and dirt from your hands.
  • Wash after workouts. Cleveland Clinic suggests washing your face soon after exercise.
  • Warm, not hot, water. The AAD says hot water and scrubbing irritate skin, and irritated skin makes pores look more noticeable.
  • Do not pick. The AAD warns against squeezing or digging at pores.

Want a moisturizer comparison for other skin types? See our Korean moisturizer guide. For the step order in general, see Korean skincare steps.

Combination skin: split the routine

Oily only in your forehead, nose and chin? That is the T-zone, and Cleveland Clinic calls this combination skin.

  • Same cleanser, toner and sunscreen on your whole face.
  • Light lotion on the T-zone, and a little more moisturizer on dry cheeks.
  • BHA only where you need it, such as the nose, not on dry patches.

Korean words for oily skin shopping

  • 지성 (ji-seong): oily skin.
  • 복합성 (bok-hap-seong): combination skin.
  • 피지 (pi-ji): sebum, skin oil.
  • 모공 (mo-gong): pores.
  • 젤 크림 (jel keu-rim): gel cream.
  • 기름종이 (gi-reum-jong-i): blotting paper.

Show the word to a staff member if you are looking for one item.

Before you buy

  • Look for "oil free" and "noncomedogenic" on the label, the AAD suggests.
  • One acid at a time. Do not start a BHA, an AHA and a retinol in the same week.
  • Acne medicines are different. Benzoyl peroxide and prescription creams are medicines. Ask a pharmacist or a dermatologist before you add one, in Seoul or at home.
  • Patch test first. Try a new product on a small spot before using it on your whole face.

item.title: Korean Skincare for Sensitive Skin: How to Choose
item.description: How to read a Korean ingredient list for sensitive skin, what 향료 and 무향 mean, fragrance-free vs. unscented, and how to patch test before your face.
item.content:encoded:
Choose Korean skincare for sensitive skin by reading the ingredient list, not the front of the box. Look for 향료, the Korean word for fragrance, pick fragrance-free over unscented, and add one product at a time. Patch test each one on your inner arm, twice a day for 7 to 10 days, before it goes on your face.

If your skin stings, flushes or itches easily, the front of a Korean box will not tell you much. Words like “calming” or “for sensitive skin” are the brand’s description. The back label is where the facts are.

Korean labels follow a clear rule for fragrance. Learn three or four words and you can check a product in a minute.

Front-label claims are not a standard

The FDA says there is no federal standard or definition for “hypoallergenic,” “fragrance-free” or “for sensitive skin” in the US. It tells shoppers to read the ingredient list instead.

Treat Korean claims the same way. 저자극 (low-irritation) and 민감 피부 (sensitive skin) on a box are the brand’s words. The ingredient list shows what is actually inside.

How fragrance shows up on a Korean label

  • The full list is called 전성분 (jeon-seong-bun). Korean products print every ingredient on the box.
  • Fragrance is often one word: 향료 (hyang-nyo). A brand can list its fragrance blend under that single word.
  • Allergens inside the fragrance must be named. If the blend contains any of 25 fragrance allergens set by the MFDS, the label cannot say only 향료. It must also name each allergen above 0.001% in a leave-on product or 0.01% in a rinse-off product (rule as of Nov. 17, 2026. Sources: MFDS guideline and Korea Cosmetic Association FAQ. Rules can change, so check the current version.)
  • Essential oils count. The MFDS guideline says plant oils or extracts used for scent must have their allergens labeled too, Cosmorning reported. A “natural” scent is still fragrance.
  • Small sizes can skip it. Minis of about 50 mL or less may leave the allergen names off the box for lack of space, but the brand must post the information online, per the same guideline.

So if you avoid fragrance, scan the list for 향료 and for names like 리날룰 (linalool) or 리모넨 (limonene).

Fragrance-free vs. unscented

These are not the same, the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) explains.

  • Fragrance-free: no fragrance, not even one you cannot smell.
  • Unscented: a fragrance is masked so you do not smell it. The AAD says the masking chemicals can irritate dry, sensitive skin.

In Korean stores you may see 무향 (mu-hyang), “no scent.” It tells you how the product smells. It does not promise there is no 향료 on the list, so check.

Patch test before your face

The AAD’s method takes 7 to 10 days. Plan for it, especially if you shop on a trip.

  • Pick a quarter-sized spot where it will not rub off, such as the inside of your arm or the bend of your elbow.
  • Apply it twice a day at your normal amount.
  • Leave it on as long as you normally would. For a cleanser, about five minutes.
  • No redness, itching or swelling after 7 to 10 days? You can use it.
  • Know the normal tingle. The AAD notes that ingredients like retinol and glycolic acid can irritate sensitive skin, and that this is often temporary.

Keep the routine short

  • One new product at a time. The AAD warns that too many products, especially several anti-aging ones, can irritate skin.
  • Go easy on exfoliating. The AAD says sensitive, dry or acne-prone skin may do best with a washcloth and a mild chemical exfoliant, not a scrub. With rosacea, it says to stop exfoliating.
  • Check your toner. A Cleveland Clinic dermatology resident advises people with sensitive skin to avoid toners that are heavily fragranced or use a lot of dyes and preservatives. Our Korean toner guide explains how toners and toner pads differ.
  • Moisturize. The AAD recommends gentle, fragrance-free products for dry, sensitive skin. See our Aestura vs. Illiyoon moisturizer guide for two Korean options, and what cica is if you keep seeing it on calming-feeling products.

A simple order to follow

Cleanser, toner if you like it, moisturizer, then sunscreen in the morning. Our Korean skincare steps guide explains why the order runs thin to thick.

Change one thing at a time. If your skin reacts, you will know which product to drop.

Korean words to look for on the back of the box

  • 전성분 (jeon-seong-bun): full ingredient list. Start here.
  • 향료 (hyang-nyo): fragrance. If you avoid fragrance, this is the word to find.
  • 리날룰 (linalool), 리모넨 (limonene), 벤질알코올 (benzyl alcohol), 신남알 (cinnamal): four of the 25 fragrance allergens Korean labels must name.
  • 무향 (mu-hyang): no scent. It describes the smell. Check the list for 향료 anyway.
  • 저자극 (jeo-ja-geuk): low-irritation, a claim the brand makes.
  • 민감 피부 (min-gam pi-bu): sensitive skin.

Screenshot this list. In a store, show it to a staff member and ask to see the back label.

Shopping in Seoul with sensitive skin

  • Photograph the back label before you buy. A translation app can read the 전성분 list for you.
  • Buy one new product, not five. You need time to patch test each one, and a trip is short.
  • Skip testers on your face. Try a store tester on your inner arm, not your cheek.
  • Medicated creams are medicines. Korean pharmacies sell ointments and creams for skin problems. Ask the pharmacist, or your dermatologist at home, before you use one. See our Korean pharmacy guide.

If your skin reacts

  • Wash it off gently as soon as you can, and do not use it again, the AAD says.
  • Soothe it. The AAD suggests a cool compress or petroleum jelly if needed.
  • See a dermatologist if the reaction is severe or does not settle.
  • Report it in the US. The FDA asks people who think they had a reaction to a cosmetic to report it to the agency and talk with their healthcare provider.

item.title: Korean Toner Guide: Toner vs. Essence vs. Skin
item.description: What a Korean toner does, why Korean stores call it 스킨 and an emulsion 로션, how toner differs from essence, and how to use toner pads without overdoing it.
item.content:encoded:
A Korean toner is a watery step you apply right after cleansing to add hydration before serum and moisturizer. Korean stores often file it under 스킨 (skin), and 로션 (lotion) there usually means a light emulsion, not body lotion. Essence is an optional, slightly richer layer, and toner pads are cotton rounds soaked in toner.

Ask for “toner” in a Seoul shop and you may be pointed to a shelf marked 스킨. Ask for “lotion” and you may get a light emulsion for your face, not a body lotion. The names are the confusing part. The step itself is simple.

What a toner is

Cleveland Clinic describes toner as a water-based liquid you use after cleansing and before moisturizing. It works like a primer for the rest of your routine.

Older Western toners often had a lot of alcohol to remove oil, which could dry and irritate skin, Cleveland Clinic notes. Newer formulas are gentler. In K-beauty, toner is usually a hydrating step, not an astringent, says Round Lab, a Korean skincare brand.

Toner is optional. Cleveland Clinic lists it as a way to step up a routine, not a must.

Three names, decoded

  • 스킨 (seu-kin) or 토너 (to-neo): toner. Sulwhasoo’s Korean store, for one, lists 스킨 as its own skincare category.
  • 로션 (ro-syeon): in Korean facial skincare, usually a light emulsion that goes after toner. Korean retailer Musinsa files it with emulsions and all-in-ones, as 로션/에멀젼/올인원.
  • 에센스 (e-sen-seu): essence, a light hydrating layer between toner and serum.

You may also see 토너/미스트 (toner and mist) as one category, as on Round Lab’s Korean store. A mist is a toner you spray.

Toner vs. essence vs. serum

They go on in that order, thinnest first.

  • Toner: the most watery. Adds a first layer of hydration after cleansing.
  • Essence: a light hydrating layer, and the easiest step to skip. Round Lab says two or three layers of a hydrating toner can cover toner, essence and a light serum.
  • Serum or ampoule: more concentrated, for one goal. See our Korean skincare steps guide for the full order.

How to use a toner

  • Right after cleansing. Swipe it on or spray it, and do not rinse it off, Cleveland Clinic says.
  • Hands or cotton. Cleveland Clinic mentions a cotton ball or round. Round Lab suggests patting a hydrating toner on.
  • Layer if you like. Patting on two or three thin layers is the Round Lab approach for extra hydration.
  • Once or twice a day. That is up to you, Cleveland Clinic says. With strong acids, start every other day.

Pick a toner by its label

Cleveland Clinic suggests matching the ingredients to what you want:

  • Dull-looking skin: AHAs or BHAs, niacinamide, or licorice root or papaya extract.
  • Mature skin: antioxidants such as vitamin C, plus hydrators like hyaluronic acid and glycerin.
  • Oily or acne-prone skin: AHAs and BHAs. A small amount of alcohol can be fine for oily skin, Cleveland Clinic says.
  • Sensitive skin: avoid toners that are heavily fragranced or use a lot of dyes and preservatives, a Cleveland Clinic dermatology resident advises. Our sensitive skin guide shows how to find fragrance on a Korean label.

Toner pads

Toner pads are cotton rounds soaked in toner, usually sold in a jar. Korean retailer Musinsa files them with toners, under 스킨/토너/패드.

  • When: after cleansing, before serum and moisturizer, Round Lab says.
  • How: swipe gently across your face in outward motions, then pat in what is left.
  • As a quick mask: Round Lab suggests leaving a pad on one area for a minute or two.
  • Rough vs. smooth side: some pads have both. The rough side exfoliates, so use it gently.

A pad with acids is an exfoliator. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) says over-exfoliating can cause redness and irritation, and the more aggressive the method, the less often you should use it.

Try it first

New toner or pad? The AAD suggests testing it on a quarter-sized spot on your inner arm, twice a day for 7 to 10 days. No redness, itching or swelling means you can move it to your face.

If your skin feels tight after cleansing, see our Korean dry skin routine for where toner fits with a richer cream.

Korean words in the toner aisle

  • 스킨 (seu-kin): toner. The everyday Korean word.
  • 토너 (to-neo): toner, the English loanword. Same step.
  • 로션 (ro-syeon): usually a light emulsion that goes after toner, not a body lotion.
  • 에멀젼 (e-meol-jyeon) or 유액 (yu-aek): emulsion.
  • 에센스 (e-sen-seu): essence.
  • 패드 (pae-deu): pad, as in toner pad.
  • 미스트 (mi-seu-teu): mist, a spray toner.

Store signs often pair them: 스킨/토너, 로션/에멀젼, 토너/미스트.

Before you buy toner pads

  • Read the ingredients for acids. AHA (such as glycolic or lactic acid) or BHA (salicylic acid) means the pad exfoliates. Cleveland Clinic says to start those every other day.
  • Check the texture. Some pads have a rough side. Round Lab, for one, says to use the rough side of its 1025 Dokdo Toner Pad on congested areas and the smooth side to hydrate.
  • Sensitive skin? The AAD says sensitive skin may do better with a mild chemical exfoliant and a washcloth than with rubbing. With rosacea, it says to stop exfoliating. See our sensitive skin guide.
  • Skip exfoliating pads on sunburned skin. The AAD says never to exfoliate a sunburn or open cuts.

Two toner routines to copy

  • Morning: cleanser, a hydrating toner patted on by hand, moisturizer, sunscreen.
  • Night: cleanser, toner pad swiped outward, toner patted in for a second layer if your skin feels tight, then moisturizer.

Using a retinoid or benzoyl peroxide? The AAD says exfoliating on top of them can worsen dryness, so keep the exfoliating pad off those nights.

item.title: Korean Makeup Tutorial: A Soft Pink Look in 7 Steps
item.description: A step-by-step Korean makeup tutorial for a soft pink, dewy look: where highlight, contour and blush go, plus palettes from Olive Young's ranking.
item.content:encoded:
Start with a thin, dewy cushion base. Shade lightly under the cheekbones and along the jaw, then sweep a sheer pink blush high on the cheeks, just under the eyes. Add a balm highlight to the cheekbones, nose bridge and chin, a soft pink palette on the lids, and a glossy gradient lip.
